narrative:
The model predicted a 67.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily in this decision were your LSAT score, your class ranking after the third year of law school, and your undergraduate GPA. Your LSAT score was by far the strongest driver, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. Scoring 23.5 compared with an average of 37.2 among accepted students created a large gap that the model saw as a major obstacle to passing the bar. Your third-year class ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure; you placed in the second decile while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. These two elements together dominated the decision.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 worked in the opposite direction, slightly lowering the predicted risk of failure, but it was not strong enough to offset the other two factors.

The school therefore concluded that, on balance, the risk of bar exam failure was too high to offer admission. To improve your chances in a future application, focus first on raising your LSAT score through intensive preparation, then work to move your class rank higher in the remaining years of law school. These two areas will have the greatest impact on how a similar model evaluates your profile next time. (218 words)
